Do the rich get richer?

New faculty co-authors gained the next year, by how many a person already has (2016–2025, pooled). The bars rise only gently: a weak, sub-linear rich-get-richer effect (almost flat at NIT Trichy). Busier people may also simply write more papers.

Faculty and links

Connected faculty (at least one faculty co-author) and links, cumulative.

Densification

Links against faculty, log–log, one point per year. A slope above 1 means links grow faster than people. Real growing networks densify the same way, with exponents from 1.08 to 1.68: citation graphs 1.56–1.68, patents 1.66, internet routers 1.18, author–paper graphs 1.08–1.15 (Leskovec, Kleinberg & Faloutsos 2005).

A giant component forms

Share of faculty in the largest connected group.

The network shrinks in distance

Effective diameter (90% of pairs within this many steps). Real growing networks do the same: distances are largest when the giant component first appears, then shrink as links are added (Leskovec et al. 2005; the separation also falls in the co-authorship networks of Barabási et al. 2002).

Departments mixed a little, then held steady

Louvain modularity and the share of cross-department links. Cross-department links rose from 24% (2016) to 30% by 2019 and have stayed at 30–32% since; modularity fell mainly because separate clusters joined up.

Do friends of friends become co-authors?

How much more likely a pair is to start working together next year than a far-apart pair (triadic closure).

Network dynamics

How things move through the faculty co-authorship network: how far an idea can spread, whether the network can fall into one rhythm, whether groups form as teams or pair by pair, which partnerships last and renew, how newcomers join, how research groups are born, merge and die, and who bridges separate groups. Both NITs; faculty-to-faculty links only.

How far can an idea spread?

SIR spreading: an idea starts with 5 faculty and each co-author passes it on with probability β (one chance per link). 1/λ₁ is the classic (SIS) epidemic threshold and a lower bound; for this SIR model the threshold is 1/λ_NB from the non-backtracking matrix (0.211 Trichy, 0.156 Surathkal; see the PDF below), and either way it is lower at Surathkal; IPR measures how concentrated the network's leading eigenvector is (high = spreading depends on a small core). Real networks are compared with degree-preserving rewired copies; simulations are the mean of 500 runs.

How the thresholds are calculated (PDF, with the formulas worked out step by step)

NIT Trichy: faculty reached

Seeding with the 5 best-connected (hubs), the 5 best bridges (betweenness), or 5 random faculty.

NIT Surathkal: faculty reached

Same seeds and β values.

Threshold and the spreading core

Can the network fall into one rhythm? (Kuramoto)

Each faculty member is an oscillator with their own natural rhythm ω (drawn from a standard normal distribution), pulled towards their co-authors' rhythm with strength K. The order parameter r runs from 0 (everyone on their own beat) to 1 (one common rhythm). Largest connected group of each network, unweighted links, 8 frequency draws per K, compared with connected degree-preserving rewired copies. Read it as how easily the network could align on a shared agenda: a model, not a measurement.

How the thresholds are calculated (PDF, K_c, the eigenratio and the worked numbers)

Synchrony as coupling grows

Solid: real network; dashed: rewired copies with the same degrees.

Who locks first

Share of faculty running at the common rhythm at K = 1, by number of faculty co-authors (both NITs).

Synchronisability

λ₂ (algebraic connectivity) and the eigenratio λ_N/λ₂ of the Laplacian: a lower eigenratio means the network synchronises more easily. Theoretical onset K_c = 2/(π g(0) λ₁) for normal frequencies; K for r = 0.5 is read from the simulations.

Teams or pairs? Faculty triangles

A triangle is three faculty who have all co-authored with each other. It is filled if one paper has all three on it (a team), and we check whether that team paper came first ("born as a team") or after the pairwise papers ("sealed later").

The six NITs side by side

Papers: OpenAlex, any author from the NIT (students' papers included), the same filter for all six. Faculty: each NIT's NIRF 2025 data file. Network: NIRF faculty matched by name to OpenAlex authors. All six are built this way, so compare them only with each other: the other tabs use our own faculty lists for each year (which also keep people who left) and hand-checked author IDs, so Trichy's a is 1.41 here but 1.61 there (Surathkal 1.74 here, 1.70 there).       By institute type

      Assortative or disassortative?

      Degree assortativity r: do well-connected nodes link to other well-connected nodes (r > 0, assortative) or to poorly connected ones (r < 0, disassortative)? Each network is compared with degree-preserving rewired copies, which keep every node's number of links and randomise only who links to whom. The institute network is shown with and without our two NITs, because as hubs of our own papers they make it disassortative partly by construction. Both NITs.

      Faculty co-authorship

      Average co-author degree knn of faculty with k co-authors (log–log). Rising = assortative.

      Institute co-authorship

      Average partner degree of institutes with k partners, with and without our two NITs. Falling = disassortative.

      Citation network

      Papers that cite k of our papers: how often the papers they cite are cited by us (mean in-degree).

      Most influential papers without self-citations

      PageRank on citations between our own papers, keeping only citations where the citing and cited papers share no author. The list with self-citations is in the Citation network tab. Both NITs.

      Which new links would help the faculty network most?

      A what-if calculation, following Barnes et al. (2026). Network efficiency is the average of 1 / distance over all pairs of faculty. We add, one at a time, the 10 new links between faculty of the same department that raise it most, and compare with 10 random links. It shows where a link would help the network, not who wants to work together. Both NITs.

      Same NIT, same department

      Across the two NITs, same department

      Network growth, link prediction and other NITs

      Average co-authors over the years and the densification exponent

      Faculty co-authorship network. Up to each year: every link formed so far. Within one year: only that year's joint papers, among faculty who published that year. The exponent a comes from links ∝ (connected faculty)a, so the average number of co-authors grows as (connected faculty)a − 1. 2026 is left out (partial year).

      Predicting new collaborations: a model trained once on 2016–2022 predicts 2023, 2024 and 2025

      Fixed model. A logistic regression learns from 2016–2022 (one-year windows 2016→2017 … 2021→2022), is given only the 2022 faculty co-authorship network, and predicts which faculty pairs write their first paper together in 2023, in 2024 and in 2025. It never sees any data after 2022. Its prediction list is its top 1% of candidate pairs (about 1,570 a year). Each year only about 1 candidate pair in 2,000 really starts working together, so exact hits are rare and precision is low; the fair comparison is a random list of the same size.

      Correct matches

      Every real new pair that is in the fixed model's top 1% for that year. Rank = its place in the list of about 1,570; the DOI is the pair's first joint paper.

      For comparison: an updated model, re-trained every year with the newest network

      Updated model (a separate method, not the one above). The same features, but re-trained every year and given the real network of the year before: 2022 for 2023, 2023 for 2024, 2024 for 2025. It shows how much the fixed model loses by not seeing faculty who joined or started publishing after 2022.
